summary: Gives IANA guidance for assigning IPv4 multicast addresses. It replaces RFC 3171 and RFC 3138 and updates RFC 2780. It is a Best Current Practice.

eli5.summary: Multicast addresses are special ones for group broadcasts. This document tells IANA how to hand them out fairly and consistently.

what is the ipv4 multicast address range for ssm
subtitle: How IANA carves up and hands out the IPv4 multicast address space, block by block.

tldr.problem: The IPv4 multicast address space is small, and IANA needed written, consistent rules for which blocks to hand out, which to leave alone and how.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC lists each multicast block with its purpose and says whether assignments follow Expert Review, IESG Approval or Standards Action, or whether no assignment policy is needed at all.
tldr.outcome: It replaces RFC 3171 and RFC 3138, updates RFC 2780, and steers new uses toward SDP/SAP, GLOP, SSM or administratively scoped space instead of fresh assignments.

today: RFC 5771 is a Best Current Practice. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it, and it obsoletes RFC 3171 and RFC 3138 and updates RFC 2780.

sections.title: Why Guidelines Are Needed
sections.content:
The Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA) allocates parameter values for protocols made or maintained by the IETF. RFC 2780 gives it guidance for newly developed protocols. This memo expands on section 4.4.2 of that RFC and tries to codify what IANA already does when it assigns IPv4 multicast addresses.

Because the IPv4 multicast address space is relatively small, the RFC recommends further assignment only in limited circumstances. IANA should assign addresses only where dynamic selection through SDP/SAP, GLOP, Source-Specific Multicast (SSM) or Administratively Scoped address spaces cannot be used. Network operators are also told to consider IPv6 multicast addresses where feasible.

The document is a revision of RFC 3171, which it obsoletes. It also obsoletes RFC 3138 and updates RFC 2780.
sections.eli5: There are only so many group addresses, so the keeper should only give out a new one when nothing else will do.

sections.title: The Registration Groups
sections.content:
Unlike IPv4 unicast, where blocks go to Regional Internet Registries, IPv4 multicast addresses are assigned directly by IANA. The RFC lists the current registration groups, from 224.0.0.0 up to 239.255.255.255. Some ranges are marked RESERVED, and applications MUST NOT use addressing in the IANA reserved blocks.

IANA generally assigns addresses from the Local Network Control, Internetwork Control and AD-HOC blocks. The other blocks (SSM, GLOP and Administratively Scoped) mostly manage themselves, as the later sections explain.

The RFC also defines its words: an allocation is a block of addresses managed by a registry for making assignments, and an assignment is a block or single address registered to an end user for a specific network or set of networks.
sections.eli5: The whole list of group addresses is split into labelled neighbourhoods. Some are in use, some are saved for later, and nobody may use the saved ones.

sections.title: Control and AD-HOC Blocks
sections.content:
The Local Network Control Block (224.0.0/24) is for protocol control traffic that is not forwarded off link. One example is OSPFIGP All Routers (224.0.0.5). The Internetwork Control Block (224.0.1/24) is for control traffic that MAY be forwarded through the Internet, such as 224.0.1.1 for NTP. Assignments in both follow an Expert Review, IESG Approval or Standards Action process.

The AD-HOC blocks I, II and III were traditionally used for applications that fit neither control block. These addresses MAY be globally routed and suit applications needing small blocks, less than a /24. IANA SHOULD NOT assign from them in general, but MAY do so under special circumstances, using the same review processes. Future assignments that do not fit the control blocks will come from AD-HOC Block III.
sections.eli5: Some addresses are for talk that stays on your street, some for talk that may travel across town, and a leftover pile for odd cases that the keeper hands out only reluctantly.

sections.title: SDP/SAP, SSM, GLOP and Scoped Blocks
sections.content:
The SDP/SAP Block (224.2/16) is used by applications that get addresses through the Session Announcement Protocol. Addresses are chosen randomly from the range not already in use, so no IANA assignment policy is required, but the block MUST NOT be used for other purposes.

The Source-Specific Multicast Block (232/8) is for SSM, an extension of IP Multicast in which traffic is forwarded to receivers only from sources they explicitly asked for. No assignment policy is needed, and the block MUST NOT be used for other purposes. The block was initially assigned to Versatile Message Transaction Protocol (VMTP) transient groups.

The GLOP Block (233/8) is globally scoped and statically assigned. A domain with a 16-bit Autonomous System Number written as X.Y gets 233.X.Y.0/24, so no IANA policy is needed. Domains with a 32-bit ASN MAY apply for AD-HOC Block III space or consider IPv6 multicast.

The Administratively Scoped Block (239/8) is for local use within a domain and needs no IANA policy. Only 256 relative offsets exist, so IANA should assign one only to a protocol that provides an infrastructure supporting service, such as the Session Announcement Protocol.
sections.eli5: Some neighbourhoods run themselves: programs pick their own address, your network number gives you one, or your company keeps its own private set. The keeper does not need to be asked.

sections.title: Retiring Extended GLOP
sections.content:
RFC 3138 had delegated to the RIRs the assignment of the part of GLOP from 233.252.0.0 to 233.255.255.255, mapped from private AS numbers 64512-65534 and the reserved ASN 65535. This space was known as Extended GLOP (EGLOP).

The RFC says RFC 3138 should not have asked the RIRs to develop policies for it, because RFC 2860 reserves that to the IETF. Making the space available to operators is important, so RFC 3138 is obsoleted and the range is classed as AD-HOC Block III.

The first /24, 233.252.0.0/24, is assigned as MCAST-TEST-NET for documentation and example code. It SHOULD be used with the domain names example.com or example.net, and addresses in it MUST NOT appear on the public Internet.
sections.eli5: An old rule let the wrong group hand out a set of addresses. This document takes that back and reserves a few for practice examples in manuals.

sections.title: Applying, Reviewing and Reclaiming
sections.content:
Requests are submitted through the application form on the IANA web site. They need enough detail for the IESG designated expert to review them, and the expert may ask for more information before assigning an address.

When several addresses are needed, they come from AD-HOC Block III. For very large requests the assignment is staged, and later stages happen only after the earlier ones are completely used. The RFC says a separate document on AD-HOC assignment policy will be developed, with format and location not yet decided.

IANA should conduct an annual review of assigned addresses. Mis-assigned addresses should be reclaimed or reassigned where possible, and assignments in the AD-HOC, DIS Transient Groups and ST Multicast Groups blocks should be reviewed to reclaim addresses not in use on the global Internet.

Temporary assignments can be renewed, but the registrant must positively ask. If IANA has no renewal request within 30 days of expiry, the assignment MUST be removed from the registry. Returned addresses MUST NOT go to anyone but the last registrant for at least one calendar year.
sections.eli5: You fill in a form, someone checks it, and once a year the keeper tidies up. If you forget to renew a loan, you lose the address, but nobody else can borrow it for a year.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC states that its assignment guidelines do not alter the security properties of either the Any Source or the Source-Specific Multicast service models. It adds nothing else on the subject. Its IANA Considerations section says only that IANA has updated its IPv4 multicast request and assignment procedures to reflect the document.
sections.eli5: This is only about how addresses are handed out, so it does not make multicast any safer or riskier.

items.label: Local Network Control
items.desc: Control traffic not forwarded off link.

items.label: Internetwork Control
items.desc: Control traffic that MAY be forwarded through the Internet.

items.label: AD-HOC Block I
items.desc: Applications that fit neither control block.

items.label: SDP/SAP
items.desc: Addresses chosen by SAP applications; no IANA policy.

items.label: AD-HOC Block II
items.desc: Applications that fit neither control block.

items.label: Source-Specific Multicast
items.desc: Reserved for SSM; no IANA policy.

items.label: AD-HOC Block III
items.desc: Future assignments that fit no other block.

items.label: Administratively Scoped
items.desc: Local use within a domain; no IANA policy.
